KEY MESSAGE 1...
A strong, closed upper low centered across the Tennessee Valley
today will begin to slide off to the northeast moving very close
overhead by early Friday morning. Coincidentally, strong surface
low pressure centered over the Carolinas will retrograde west
and occluding underneath the upper low. A tight surface 
gradient between the low and a high positioned near Maine, 
coupled with an anomalously strong low-level jet in exceedance 
of 99th percentile climatology, will result in windy conditions 
today. The strongest gusts will be felt in the higher elevation
of both PA and WV with some of those gusts leaking down into the
surrounding lower elevation just to the west. This is likely 
being driven by two primary factors:

The first being an increased likelihood of breaking mountain 
waves spilling farther west/ridgetops being within the core of 
the LLJ. In the ridges, REFS probability for High Wind Warning 
criteria gusts >58 mph is 80-100%, >70 mph 60-80%, and a narrow
corridor of 50+% for >80 mph in the ridgetops of Preston and 
Tucker Counties as these ridgetops sit solidly within the core 
of a screaming 70-80 knot jet being sampled by nearby VAD
profiles around 1.5-2.5 kft. One wrinkle that may be at least
delaying the highest gusts in the PA ridges, and also the slight
decrease in overall gust probability there, is flow taking on a
bit more easterly component than forecast rather than southeast.
This is a less favorable wind direction relative to the
orientation of the terrain for breaking mountain waves. Hi res
guidance still indicates some southeasterly veering this
afternoon and enhancement of gusts. That said, for the highest 
terrain above 1800 feet, we shouldn't really be reliant on
mountain waves for the strongest wind as that elevation will be
solidly within the core of the LLJ. As such, no changes to the
ongoing wind headlines are warranted.

Farther west, swaths of REFS probability for Advisory criteria 
gusts >46 mph are up to 80% into Indiana, Jefferson, 
Westmoreland, and Fayette Counties, so the Wind Advisory remains
in effect there. Still wouldn't rule out those gusts even 
farther west where REFS probability has increased into Butler, 
Allegheny, Washington, and Greene Counties, though have less 
confidence there. In fact, those areas might be driven by the 
second factor...

The second factor is more resultant of mixing than downslope 
wind or residence within the LLJ core. Near-surface thermal 
profiles aren't necessarily stable as much as they are 
isothermal conditionally unstable at times within a saturated 
boundary layer beneath the warm advection-driven inversion. 
This could allow for a coincident occurrence of higher wind 
gusts mixing down within the heaviest rain as the mixed layer
should extend high enough to tap into the elevated wind aloft. 
In general, expect that peak easterly wind gusts will range from
35-45 mph in the lower elevations. The window of impact shifts
north through the afternoon coincident with the northward
movement of the low-level jet.

Wind subsides during the late afternoon/evening hours as the
surface low pivots and begins lifting northeast, though gusts
will continue in the ridges. Another round of gusty wind is
expected on Friday with cold advection steepening lapse rates in
low-level south-southwest (yes) flow. While momentum transfer 
won't be near as potent as Thursday, we'll still have 25-30 
knots to mix down and a pressure gradient on the back side of 
the departing low. Probability for >30 mph gusts ranges from 
50-90%, highest in WV and PA, but >40 mph drops off rapidly to 
20-40% in the lowlands. Eastern Tucker County hangs on to >80% 
probability for Advisory criteria gusts potentially through 
Friday night, so an extension of wind headlines there will be 
evaluated in the next 12-18 hours.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The aforementioned low pressure system will draw upon Atlantic 
waters to result in widespread rain for a large portion of the 
day Thursday into Friday morning. Precipitable water values rise
up to above the 90th percentile of climatology through the day
on Thursday. Expect that it'll be a steady rain through the
mid-afternoon hours, save the immediate westerly slopes of the
ridges where downsloping rain shadow effects will result in 
localized lighter rain. As such, there will likely be a minimum
in rain amounts along the western slope of the higher elevation
in PA down to WV. Conversely, a pivoting, stronger area of 
850-700 mb frontogenesis, and an overall longer period of rain 
as a backside surface trough slowly pivots through, is likely to
drive an area of higher amounts in eastern OH. Think that this
corridor is likely to stretch from Youngstown down to Coshocton
to Zanesville given progged area of frontogenesis maximum and
convergence along the nose of the departing LLJ. The heaviest 
of the rain is expected through the mid-afternoon before drier 
air evident on water vapor imagery wraps in from the south
